chunks: Substrate twice as thick: impedance impact and fixes.
The question: I have a two-layer PCB built but when I get it, the manufacturer made a mistake and the substrate layer is twice as thick as it should be.
How does this impact the characteristic impedance? What could I do to fix it?
Impedance of a trace goes up when the insulating layer between the trace and its ground plane gets thicker.
The trace then has less capacitance to the plane, and a larger current loop. So a board built with a substrate twice as thick has a higher impedance than designed.
Against a 50 ohms system, the mismatch reflects part of the signal. Whether that matters depends on how fast the edges are compared with the trace length.
Imagine a hose carrying water pulses. If the hose suddenly gets narrower in the middle, some of the water bounces back.
A thicker substrate is like that narrower section: the trace is the same width, but the "grip" on the ground plane is weaker. A short hose with slow pulses hardly notices.
A long hose with sharp pulses does.
The orange curve is the same family shifted up. At the designed width (1. 52 mm) the impedance jumps from 50 to 72.
6 ohms; to get back to 50 ohms on the thick substrate the trace must be about 3. 07 mm wide, twice as wide.
Dielectric height ( h ): the distance from the trace to its reference plane. On a two-layer board, it is the core thickness.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): rises with h and falls with trace width ("Changing a trace's characteristic impedance").
Reflection coefficient ( ): (Z 2 minus Z 1) over (Z 2 plus Z 1) ("Sources of reflection on a PCB and fixes").
Return loss: -20 log , how far below the incident wave the reflection is.
Electrical length: whether the trace delay is more than about a sixth of the rise time ("Rules of thumb for routing high-speed signals").
A 50 ohms microstrip is built with a 1. 517 mm trace on 0. 8 mm FR-4. The fab makes the core 1. 6 mm. The impedance rises to about 72. 6 ohms. Against 50 ohms, equals (72.
6 minus 50) over (72. 6 plus 50) equals 0. 184 , about a 15 decibels return loss. A 2 nanoseconds edge on a 50 mm trace hides this. A 500 picoseconds edge shows it.
That is the whole idea.
"Doubling the substrate thickness lowers the trace's capacitance to the plane and raises its loop inductance, so Z 0 goes up by about 45%: a 50 ohms trace on a 0.
8 mm core becomes about 73 ohms at 1. 6 mm. That gives about 0. 18 against 50 ohms. If the trace is electrically short for the edge rate I may live with it.
Otherwise the best fix is to have the board remade; else I re-terminate for the real impedance, slow the edges, or hand-widen the critical traces to about 3 mm or add grounded coplanar copper."
